data.content_ref: inline:The target identifies the suppression of evapotranspiration and latent heat loss as the single governing mechanism for the nocturnal UHI and its cross-city variation, while largely omitting the release of sensible heat stored in urban thermal mass during the day. Urban materials (concrete, asphalt) absorb large amounts of solar radiation during daytime and have high heat capacity; after sunset, they slowly release this stored sensible heat via longwave radiation and convection, which is a primary driver of why urban air stays several degrees warmer on a clear, calm night. By framing latent heat suppression as the single best explanation, the answer under-accounts for this dominant nocturnal energy release, especially under the clear, calm conditions specified (which maximize longwave radiative cooling differences and stored-heat release).
